### Stateful hash-based signatures (LMS/HSS) security issues

Douglas reported another incoming report relating to LMS/HSS, adding to a cluster of reports received over the past month and a half. Working in the private security-tracking repository, he consolidated these down to two patches with a plan to publish a new advisory for each, acknowledging the various submitters (Trail of Bits and a couple of others). The work is tracked under coordination meta-issue #65, with issues #63 and #64 holding the two patches and their draft advisories; Douglas tagged Norman for review. Norman confirmed he has started and has a couple of suggested changes he is testing before posting.

Norman raised a design concern about one of the patches. When stateful hash-based signatures were integrated, the team decided (late in the integration process) to disable key generation and signature generation, leaving liboqs effectively verification-only. Because LMS/XMSS admit a very large number of parameter/layer combinations (up to 8 layers, of which OQS implemented only two), one of the proposed fixes would restrict verification to exactly those variants for which OQS supports key and signature generation — which, since generation is disabled by default, would in Norman's view substantially diminish the usefulness of the verification path. Douglas responded that liboqs does not expose a generic "verify any LMS-shaped signature" entry point: the API is per-variant, specifying the number of levels and hash configuration, with a corresponding verify algorithm, so arbitrary verification of unsupported variants is not offered. Rodrigo added that the same argument extends to the provider, where only the requested supported variants are exercised. Norman noted the nuance that at the provider level the exposed API is generic-looking (there is no stateful-hash-based-signature-specific API surfaced to the provider), and agreed to write the concern up in the repository so the discussion can continue there.

Rodrigo also flagged the public [PR #2507](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2507) (out-of-bounds read in `hss_validate_signature_init`), which he suspected relates to items in the security-tracking repository. Douglas later confirmed it does appear related to the private issues and will pull them together; because this one is already public, he wants the corresponding advisory (security-tracking issue #64) landed relatively sooner, and asked Norman to review it and comment there on whether it carries the verification-scope concern he raised.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Norman):** Write up the verification-scope concern (restricting verification to generatable LMS/HSS variants) on the security-tracking repository, and review/comment on security-tracking issue #64, including whether [PR #2507](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2507) shares that concern.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Douglas):** Consolidate the public [PR #2507](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2507) with the related private LMS/HSS issues and land the corresponding advisory relatively sooner, given the public exposure.

### CodeQL and OpenSSL return code handling — [PR #2415](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2415)

Bruce introduced [PR #2415](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2415), which adds a CodeQL query enforcing OpenSSL return code handling. The broader question it raises is whether and how OQS wants to use CodeQL at all: the GitHub *default* setup is currently enabled for liboqs and produces a very large volume of results, many of them false positives or out of scope because the scanned code is not owned by liboqs. The alternatives are the *advanced* setup — maintaining an OQS-specific CodeQL workflow YAML in GitHub Actions, for which GitHub provides a reasonable template — or having someone with access to the security scanning install CodeQL locally, run it, and upload the artifact manually. Bruce did not expect consensus in this meeting; he plans to leave the PR alone for at least a week and revisit next week when more liboqs stakeholders are present, possibly taking a vote.

Norman asked whether adhering to OpenSSL return code conventions is appropriate given that many liboqs users do not use the provider, and there is precedent for not following OpenSSL conventions except when building with the OpenSSL flag. Bruce and Rodrigo clarified that this is purely an additional CI check applied to liboqs builds that use OpenSSL as the underlying cryptographic backend — no change to liboqs's own return code system and no external behaviour change. In liboqs, OpenSSL is an alternative backend for shared components (symmetric primitives, random bytes, some memory functions) abstracted behind `OQS_SHA3`/`OQS_MEM_*`-style APIs, with a normalisation layer, so behaviour across the OQS API barrier is identical regardless of backend. Norman noted his concern stems from OpenSSL historically being inconsistent in its return codes and their meanings. Bruce and Rodrigo observed that liboqs pins a fixed OpenSSL version and does not aim to test OpenSSL, unlike the provider, which by design tests against OpenSSL master and is consequently exposed to the churn in current OpenSSL development around how providers are constructed and how things are stored.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (liboqs maintainers):** Review [PR #2415](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2415) and form a view on whether/how OQS should use CodeQL (default setup, advanced setup with an OQS-maintained workflow, or manual local runs), for discussion — possibly a vote — at next week's status meeting.

### Pre-commit hooks — [PR #2446](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2446)

Bruce's second item was [PR #2446](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2446), nominally Markdown linting, but the point he wanted to raise is the introduction of pre-commit hooks into liboqs. Git runs the configured script at `git commit` time, which is a good fit for lightweight coding conventions — Python and C linters and auto-formatters — that today are only caught by the push tests in GitHub Actions, five or six minutes after a push. There is a one-time client-side setup cost, which Bruce documented in a new section of CONTRIBUTING.md; it is a single Git command pointing at a script already committed to the branch. The mechanism is entirely opt-in (contributors who skip it simply rely on CI as before) and has an escape hatch in `--no-verify`, making it in Bruce's view a low-risk way to shift lightweight tests earlier, give contributors quicker feedback, and save some pipeline CPU minutes. He noted pre-commit hooks are standard practice on many large projects and asked maintainers, especially those unfamiliar with them, to take a look.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (liboqs maintainers):** Review [PR #2446](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2446) and the proposal to adopt pre-commit hooks, commenting offline or ready for live discussion next week.
